title: Knowing God and ourselves
hookLine: Calvin's Institutes begin: true wisdom is knowing God and knowing ourselves

lines: THE INSTITUTES OF THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION.
cards: How do you open a book meant to explain the whole Christian faith? With God's attributes? With the creation of the world?
With a proof? John Calvin wrote that kind of book, the Institutes of the Christian Religion, and kept reworking it through his life. And its very first move isn't about God alone.
In paraphrase: nearly all the wisdom we have, true and solid wisdom, comes down to two parts. Knowing God, and knowing ourselves. Two knowledges, braided together from the first sentence.

teach.h: WHICH COMES FIRST? HARD TO SAY.
teach.b: Then Calvin admits something unexpected. The two are so tied together, he says, that it isn't easy to tell which comes first. Look one way.
When people take an honest look at themselves, they find need: things they lack, wrongs they've done, limits they can't get past.
And that very lack, Calvin says, sends them looking for God, the way an empty cup points to water. Now look the other way. We never see ourselves clearly, he says, until we've first looked at God.

teach.h: NEXT TO THE LIGHT, OUR OWN SHAPE.
teach.b: Next to the light, we finally see our own shape. Self-knowledge pushes toward God; knowledge of God shows us ourselves. Calvin didn't invent the pairing.
It runs through the Psalms. One asks, in the King James Bible: "What is man, that thou art mindful of him?"
Another prays: "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts." Someone asking God to do the looking, because they can't fully see themselves.
Paul says that for now we know in part, and one day "then shall I know even as also I am known." Calvin wrote in Latin, and his word for this knowledge was cognitio.
In the Reformed tradition the Institutes is read as a foundational book. Lutheran, Catholic and Orthodox Christians read him with different questions, and disagree with him on many things.
But his opening move is one anyone can try: look honestly at yourself, and notice where the looking leads.

how: Reformed and Presbyterian Christians study Calvin's Institutes in seminaries and church study groups, and its opening on knowing God and ourselves is a familiar starting point for reflection.

games.q: you're Calvin, writing the opening of a book meant to explain the whole Christian faith. where do you start?
o: with a list of God's attributes.
with the creation of the world.
with knowing God and knowing ourselves, together.
games.why: he opened with the two knowledges, and admitted it's hard to say which comes first.

practice: Sit quietly and ask yourself, gently, for one thing that's true about you right now: not the most flattering, not the harshest, just true, something you need, something you're carrying, something you're good at and rarely admit.
When it comes, don't argue with it. If you pray, offer it to God the way the psalm does, search me; if you don't, simply sit with it honestly.

wordCard.voice: Cognitio. Calvin's Latin word for knowledge: the opening move of his Institutes, that knowing God and knowing ourselves lead into each other.

orig.note: Latin: knowledge, recognition. Calvin wrote the Institutes in Latin.
